question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Back against the wall
option_1: Be in an easy situation from where escape is difficult
option_2: Be in a difficult situation from where escape is difficult
option_3: Be in a relationship which one wants to escape
option_4: Be in a difficult situation from where escape is easy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Be in a difficult situation from where escape is difficult.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Back against the wall" means to be in a very difficult or desperate situation from which escape or manoeuvring is difficult, leaving no choice but to fight or resist. (मुश्किल हालात में फंसा होना)
◦ Example: With his back against the wall, he had no option but to accept the deal.

• The idiom draws its imagery from a person literally standing with their back touching a wall, unable to retreat any further, and thus forced to defend themselves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Be in an easy situation from where escape is difficult" is incorrect because the idiom refers to a difficult, not easy, situation.

• Option 3: "Be in a relationship which one wants to escape" is incorrect because the idiom is general and not restricted to relationships.

• Option 4: "Be in a difficult situation from where escape is easy" is incorrect because the whole point of the idiom is that escape is not easy.

NOTE

• Other idioms describing difficult situations often asked in SSC: "Between the devil and the deep sea" (caught between two dangers), "Between a rock and a hard place" (forced to choose between two unpleasant options), and "In deep water" (in serious trouble).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
His house was filthy with papers and eatables strewn everywhere.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Clean.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "filthy" means extremely dirty or unclean. (गंदा)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Clean", meaning free from dirt, marks, or mess. (साफ़)
◦ Example: After the renovation, the house looked spotlessly clean.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Dignified" means having or showing a composed, serious manner worthy of respect — unrelated to cleanliness, so it is not an antonym of "filthy".

• Option 2: "Integral" means necessary or essential to make something whole — it has no relation to dirt or cleanliness.

• Option 3: "Barren" means unproductive or bare — this describes emptiness, not cleanliness, so it is not an antonym of "filthy".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "filthy": squalid, grimy, soiled, unclean.

• Other antonym pairs often asked: dirty–clean, messy–tidy, foul–pure.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
She is laughing at me.
option_1: I am being laughed at by her.
option_2: I have been laughed by her.
option_3: I was being laughed at by her.
option_4: I had been laughed by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I am being laughed at by her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "She is laughing at me" is in the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "me" becomes the subject "I"; the auxiliary becomes "am being" (to agree with "I"); the verb "laughing at" becomes "laughed at"; and "she" becomes the agent "by her".
◦ Passive: I am being laughed at by her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "have been laughed by" is the passive of the Present Perfect Tense, and it also drops the required preposition "at".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was being laughed at" is the passive of the Past Continuous Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "had been laughed by" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, and it also drops the preposition "at".

NOTE

• With verbs like "laugh at", "look at", "listen to", the preposition must be retained immediately after the verb in the passive voice.

• Present Continuous passive always uses the structure "is/am/are + being + V3".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
He was uncomfortable at the sport event.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Easeful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "uncomfortable" means feeling physical or mental unease or awkwardness. (असहज)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Easeful", meaning characterised by ease and comfort. (सहज, आरामदायक)
◦ Example: She felt easeful and relaxed in the company of old friends.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Difficult" is not related to comfort or ease — it describes hardship in general, not the opposite of "uncomfortable".

• Option 3: "Awkward" is actually a synonym of "uncomfortable" (feeling ill at ease), not its antonym.

• Option 4: "Troublesome" means causing trouble or difficulty — this is also close in meaning to "uncomfortable", not opposite to it.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "uncomfortable": awkward, troubled, uneasy, self-conscious.

• Other antonym pairs: comfortable–uncomfortable, ease–unease, relaxed–tense.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in past tense form.
The declarations which come out from that office are not dependable.
option_1: The declarations which will come out from that office may not be dependable.
option_2: The declarations which come out from that office were not dependable.
option_3: The declarations which came out from that office are not dependable.
option_4: The declarations which came out from that office were not dependable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The declarations which came out from that office were not dependable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The declarations which come out from that office are not dependable" is in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — changing Simple Present to Simple Past: every verb in the sentence must be converted to its past form — "come" becomes "came" (V2), and "are" becomes "were".

• Applying the rule to both clauses: the relative clause verb "come out" becomes "came out", and the main verb "are" becomes "were".
◦ Past form: The declarations which came out from that office were not dependable.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will come" and "may" express future possibility, not past tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes only the main verb ("were") to past but leaves the relative clause verb "come out" in the present tense — both verbs must agree in tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it changes only the relative clause verb ("came out") to past but leaves the main verb "are" in the present tense.

NOTE

• When a sentence has a relative clause ("which/who/that..."), both the main clause verb and the relative clause verb must be changed consistently when the tense of the sentence is changed.

• Simple Present → Simple Past: V1/V5 → V2; is/am/are → was/were.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The management is not beware of this fact.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. aware of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "beware" is used only in the imperative mood (e.g., "Beware of the dog") or after modal verbs like "must/should" (e.g., "You must beware of strangers"). It is never used with "is/am/are/was/were" as an ordinary descriptive verb.

• To describe a state of knowing or being conscious of a fact, the correct adjective phrase is "aware of", used with a form of "be" (is/am/are/was/were).

• Applying the rule: since the sentence uses "is not" before the underlined segment, "beware of" must be replaced with the grammatically correct "aware of".
◦ Corrected: The management is not aware of this fact.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "awaking to" means becoming conscious of something gradually, but it does not fit idiomatically after "is not" and changes the intended meaning.

• Option 3: "beware to" is grammatically wrong — "beware" is followed by the preposition "of", never "to", and cannot in any case follow "is not".

• Option 4: "watchful with" is incorrect because "watchful" takes the preposition "of" or "for", not "with", and does not fit the sense of "not knowing a fact".

NOTE

• Common confusion: "beware" (a warning verb, used in imperative/modal constructions) vs "aware" (an adjective describing knowledge of a fact, used with "be" verbs).

• Similarly confused pairs: "afraid of" vs "scared of", "conscious of" vs "cognizant of".

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Prophane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Profane", meaning showing disrespect for sacred things, or (of language) coarse and offensive.
◦ Example: He was asked to leave the temple for using profane language.

• Spelling key: PRO + FANE — note there is no "ph"; the word begins with "Pro-", not "Proph-".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reasonable" is correctly spelt — meaning fair and sensible.

• Option 2: "Laughable" is correctly spelt — meaning deserving to be laughed at, ridiculous.

• Option 3: "Blessed" is correctly spelt — meaning made holy or fortunate.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "profane" with "prophecy"/"prophet", which genuinely contain "ph" because they derive from Greek "pro + phanai" (to speak); "profane" instead comes from Latin "pro + fanum" (outside the temple).

• Other commonly confused spellings: "Definitely" (not "Definately"), "Occurrence" (not "Occurence"), "Rhythm" (not "Rythm").

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A detailed description of a series of real or fictional events taking place over a long period of time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Saga.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Saga" means a detailed description of a series of real or fictional events taking place over a long period of time, often a long story of heroic achievement or family history. (एक लंबी गाथा या कथा)
◦ Example: The novel narrates the saga of three generations of a farming family.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Witness" (गवाह) means a person who sees an event happen, or gives evidence in court — not a long narrative.

• Option 2: "Journal" (पत्रिका/दैनिकी) means a periodical publication, or a personal daily record — it is not necessarily a long narrative of events over time.

• Option 4: "Case study" (मामले का अध्ययन) means a detailed analysis of a single specific instance, not a long narrative of events over time.

NOTE

• Similar one-word substitutes: "Chronicle" (a factual written account of events in order of time), "Epic" (a long poem narrating heroic deeds), "Memoir" (a personal account of one's own life/experiences).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who compiles a dictionary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Lexicographer.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Lexicographer" means a person who compiles dictionaries. (शब्दकोश लेखक)
◦ Example: Samuel Johnson, the famous lexicographer, published his dictionary in 1755.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Plagiarist" (साहित्यिक चोर) means a person who copies another person's work and passes it off as their own — unrelated to dictionaries.

• Option 2: "Iconoclast" (मूर्तिभंजक) means a person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditional institutions — unrelated to dictionary-making.

• Option 3: "Bibliophile" (पुस्तक प्रेमी) means a person who loves or collects books — not necessarily someone who compiles dictionaries.

NOTE

• Related word-building profession terms often asked: "Cartographer" (map maker), "Biographer" (one who writes another's life story), "Etymologist" (one who studies word origins).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'Sophisticated' from the given sentence.
The tribe had no access to modern technology or resources and had to rely on primitive tools and techniques for survival.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Primitive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Sophisticated" means highly developed, complex, and refined, especially in technology or design. (परिष्कृत, उन्नत)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Primitive", meaning basic, undeveloped, or belonging to an early, simple stage. (आदिम, अविकसित)
◦ Example: The islanders still used primitive fishing methods, unlike the sophisticated trawlers used elsewhere.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Technology" is a noun referring to the tools/machinery itself — it is not an adjective and cannot be an antonym of "sophisticated".

• Option 3: "Modern" actually tends to be associated with sophistication (modern technology is often sophisticated), so it is not an opposite.

• Option 4: "Techniques" is a plain noun for methods, not an antonym of "sophisticated".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "sophisticated": advanced, refined, complex, cultured.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested: advanced–backward, refined–crude, complex–simple.

question:
Read the given sentence and select the most appropriate synonym of the word 'Vigilant' from the following options.
The burglar was very cautious, so he avoided the security perfectly as they didn't find any proof.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. cautious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Vigilant" means keeping careful watch for possible danger or difficulty; watchful and alert. (सतर्क, सावधान)

• Its most appropriate synonym among the options is "cautious", meaning careful to avoid danger or mistakes. (सावधान)
◦ Example: The vigilant/cautious guard checked every visitor's identity before letting them in.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "proof" means evidence establishing a fact — unrelated in meaning to "vigilant".

• Option 3: "burglar" means a person who commits burglary (a thief) — it is a noun referring to a person, not a synonym of the adjective "vigilant".

• Option 4: "security" means the state of being protected, or the protective staff/system itself — it does not mean "watchful" in the way "vigilant" does.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "vigilant": alert, watchful, wary, observant, on guard.

• Antonym of "vigilant": negligent, careless, inattentive.

question:
Choose the ANTONYM of the word 'effervescent' in the given sentence.
Sonali is bubbly and carefree in comparison to her sister Mitali's subdued nature.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Subdued.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "effervescent" means vivacious and enthusiastic; bubbling with high spirits. (उत्साह से भरपूर, जोशीला)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Subdued", meaning quiet, restrained, or lacking liveliness. (दबा हुआ, शांत)
◦ Example: Unlike her effervescent sister, Mitali had a subdued and reserved nature.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Bubbly" is actually a synonym of "effervescent" (both mean lively/cheerful), not its antonym.

• Option 2: "Comparison" is a plain noun meaning the act of comparing — it has no relation in meaning to "effervescent".

• Option 3: "Carefree" means free from worry, which is close in spirit to "effervescent" (both describe a light, happy disposition), not opposite to it.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "effervescent": bubbly, vivacious, exuberant, ebullient.

• Other antonym pairs: vivacious–dull, exuberant–lifeless, animated–subdued.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The case of Vanuatu in 2020 is a clear example of the constant and complex challenges faced by SIDS. It shows how SIDS are dealing with multiple crises at the same time and how COVID-19 has particularly exposed SIDS' extreme and interlinked vulnerabilities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. interlaced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "interlinked" means connected together, joined so that one affects the other. (परस्पर जुड़ा हुआ)

• Its most appropriate synonym is "interlaced", meaning woven or linked together intricately. (आपस में गुंथा हुआ)
◦ Example: The economic and social vulnerabilities of small island nations are deeply interlaced/interlinked.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "continuous" means happening without interruption — it describes duration, not the sense of things being connected to one another.

• Option 2: "severe" means very great or serious (in degree) — it describes intensity, not interconnection.

• Option 3: "free" means not connected or restricted — this is close to the opposite of "interlinked".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "interlinked": interconnected, intertwined, interwoven, interdependent.

• The passage's context (COVID-19 exposing multiple, connected vulnerabilities of Small Island Developing States, SIDS) supports "interlaced" as the best fit meaning "linked together".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given word.
Harangue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A lengthy and aggressive speech.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Harangue" means a lengthy and aggressive speech, typically a lecture or scolding delivered forcefully. (लंबा और आक्रामक भाषण/डांट)
◦ Example: The coach gave the team a harangue after their poor performance in the match.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Strict disciplinarian" (कठोर अनुशासक) describes a person who enforces strict rules — this is the meaning of a different word, "disciplinarian", not "harangue".

• Option 2: "Breaker of idols" (मूर्तिभंजक) is the meaning of "iconoclast", not "harangue".

• Option 3: "Airplane shed" (विमान शेड) is the meaning of "hangar", a word that merely sounds similar to "harangue" but is unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• "Harangue" can function as both a noun (a forceful speech) and a verb (to lecture someone forcefully).

• Similar-sounding but different words often confused in SSC vocabulary: hangar (aircraft shed) vs harangue (aggressive speech).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.
The river (flowing) under the bridge.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. flows.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The river (flowing) under the bridge" has no finite (tensed) main verb, so the bracketed word "flowing" (a participle) must be replaced with a proper finite verb to complete the sentence.

• Rule: a simple statement describing a general, ongoing fact (a river's regular flow) is expressed in the Simple Present Tense, using Subject + V1/V5.

• Applying the rule: the subject "The river" is third person singular, so the verb takes the "-s" form.
◦ Corrected: The river flows under the bridge.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was flow" is incorrect because "was" (a past tense auxiliary) cannot combine with the base form "flow"; it would need a participle ("was flowing").

• Option 3: "is flow" is incorrect for the same reason — "is" must be followed by a present participle ("is flowing"), not the bare base form "flow".

• Option 4: "is flowed" is incorrect because "flow" is an intransitive verb and cannot be used in the passive voice ("is flowed").

NOTE

• A sentence needs at least one finite verb; a participle alone ("flowing", "flown") cannot serve as the main verb of a simple sentence without an auxiliary.

• Intransitive verbs (flow, occur, happen, arrive) cannot be used in the passive voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
They have disposed all the old books.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. disposed of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "dispose" is always followed by the preposition "of" when it means "to get rid of something, or to deal with/finish something".

• Rule: "Dispose" is never used as a plain transitive verb directly followed by an object (e.g., "disposed all the old books" is grammatically incorrect); it must take the object through the preposition "of".

• Applying the rule: "the old books" is the object that must follow "disposed" through the preposition "of".
◦ Corrected: They have disposed of all the old books.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "disposed out" is incorrect; "dispose" does not idiomatically combine with the preposition "out".

• Option 3: "disposed on" is incorrect; "dispose" does not idiomatically combine with the preposition "on" in this sense.

• Option 4: "disposed by" is incorrect; "by" would indicate an agent (as in passive voice), which does not fit this active-voice sentence.

NOTE

• Other verbs that must be followed by a specific preposition before their object: "deal with", "cope with", "consist of", "result in".

• "Dispose of" means to get rid of or finish dealing with something; note the different meaning of "disposed to" (inclined/willing to do something), e.g., "He is disposed to help."

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To prime the pump
option_2: Encourage the growth or action of something'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Encourage the growth or action of something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To prime the pump" means to stimulate or encourage the growth or activity of something, especially by an initial input of effort or money. (किसी चीज़ को शुरूआती मदद देकर बढ़ावा देना)
◦ Example: The government decided to prime the pump of the economy by increasing public spending.

• The idiom comes from the literal act of pouring a small amount of water into an old-style hand pump before use, to create the suction needed to draw up more water.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Manipulate someone to achieve success" is incorrect; the idiom is about stimulating growth, not manipulating people.

• Option 3: "To use a pump efficiently" takes the phrase too literally; the idiom is figurative and refers to encouraging growth, not the literal efficient use of a water pump.

• Option 4: "Ask others to be ambitious" is incorrect; the idiom does not concern encouraging ambition in others.

NOTE

• Other economy/growth-related idioms often asked in SSC: "Kick-start" (to give initial impetus to something), "Grease the wheels" (to make something happen more smoothly), "Jump-start" (to give something a quick boost to get it going).

question:
The sentence given below has one misspelt word. Spot the INCORRECTLY spelt word and select its correct spelling.
Last-bench students are mysterous by nature.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mysterious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The misspelt word in the sentence is "mysterous"; its correct spelling is "Mysterious", meaning difficult or impossible to understand, explain, or identify.
◦ Example: The last-bench students are mysterious by nature.

• Spelling key: MYS + TER + I + OUS. Note the "i" before "ous", which is often mistakenly dropped.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Mystirious" is incorrect; the second vowel should be "e" (as in "myster-"), not "i".

• Option 2: "Misterous" is incorrect; it drops the required "y" after "M" and the "i" before "-ous".

• Option 4: "Misterious" is incorrect; the first vowel should be "y" (as in "Mys-"), not "i".

NOTE

• Related words: "mystery" (noun), "mysteriously" (adverb).

• Other commonly misspelt "-ious" ending words: "Curious", "Serious", "Various", "Glorious".

question:
Select the grammatically correct sentence.
A. It is a old uniform but a memorable thing for me.
B. It is old uniform but a memorable thing for me.
C. It is the old uniform but memorable thing for me.
D. It is an old uniform but a memorable thing for me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. D.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — use of the indefinite article "an": the article "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound, including words like "old", "hour", "honest" (where the initial sound is a vowel sound).

• Since "old" begins with the vowel sound /oʊ/, it must be preceded by "an", not "a"; also, since "uniform" and "thing" are singular countable nouns being mentioned for the first time (not one specific, already-known item), both need an indefinite article.

• Applying the rule: "It is an old uniform but a memorable thing for me" correctly uses "an" before "old" and "a" before "memorable thing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (Sentence D).

Additional Information

• Sentence A: "It is a old uniform..." is incorrect because "a" is wrongly used before the vowel sound "old"; it should be "an old".

• Sentence B: "It is old uniform..." is incorrect because the singular countable noun "uniform" needs an article ("an old uniform"), which is missing.

• Sentence C: "It is the old uniform but memorable thing..." is incorrect because "the" wrongly implies one specific, already-known uniform, and the noun phrase "memorable thing" is missing its required article "a".

NOTE

• "An" is used before a vowel sound, not merely a vowel letter — e.g., "an hour" (silent h) but "a university" (starts with the /j/ sound, a consonant sound).

• Other tricky examples: "an heir", "an honest man", "a European", "a one-rupee coin".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The audience loved her performance.
option_1: The audience will love her performance.
option_2: The performance is loved by the audience.
option_3: Her performance was loved by the audience.
option_4: The performance was loved by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Her performance was loved by the audience.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The audience loved her performance" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "her performance" becomes the subject; it is singular, so the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "loved" becomes the past participle "loved" (V3); and "the audience" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: Her performance was loved by the audience.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will love" is future tense, not the passive of the given past-tense sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is loved" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because the subject and object have been interchanged wrongly: "the audience" (the original subject/agent) has wrongly become the new object, producing a meaning where "the performance" — not "her performance" — is loved by "her" (the original object).

NOTE

• Possessive adjectives attached to the object ("her performance") must be carried over unchanged into the passive subject.

• Simple Past passive always uses the structure "was/were + V3".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Redwing had read (1)________ that one of his favourite writers, Ernest Hemingway, had been asked what was the best (2)________ for a novelist. He had said “an unhappy childhood”. Redwing had enjoyed a fine time growing up, but he (3)________ if this whole (4)________ was unfolding more like a novel, and would be (5)________ on one person, one character, the guy in charge: him. Maybe you got a happy childhood and then an unhappy adulthood, and that’s how novels worked.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. somewhere.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Redwing had read ________ that one of his favourite writers, Ernest Hemingway, had been asked what was the best training for a novelist." The blank needs an adverb indicating an unspecified, unknown place/source where Redwing came across this piece of information.

• "Somewhere" is the correct fit because it means "in or at some unspecified place", matching the vague, unrecalled source of information typical of casual reading or recollection.

• Applying the rule: "had read somewhere" is a common collocation meaning "had come across in some unspecified reading material".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "wholesome" is an adjective meaning conducive to physical or moral well-being — it cannot grammatically follow "had read" as an adverb of place.

• Option 2: "negligently" is an adverb of manner meaning carelessly — it does not fit the sense of an unspecified place/source.

• Option 4: "careless" is an adjective, not an adverb, and does not fit grammatically or contextually after "had read".

NOTE

• "Somewhere", "anywhere", "nowhere", and "everywhere" are compound adverbs of place commonly tested in cloze passages.

• Watch for part-of-speech mismatches in cloze options — an adjective (careless, wholesome) cannot correctly fill a slot that grammatically requires an adverb.

Redwing had enjoyed a fine time growing up, but he (3)________ if this whole (4)________ was unfolding more like a novel, and would be (5)________ on one person, one character, the guy in charge: him. Maybe you got a happy childhood and then an unhappy adulthood, and that’s how novels worked.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. training.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...one of his favourite writers, Ernest Hemingway, had been asked what was the best ________ for a novelist. He had said 'an unhappy childhood'." The answer "an unhappy childhood" makes sense only as a response to a question about the best preparation/grounding for becoming a novelist.

• "Training" fits because it means preparation or development through instruction and experience for a particular role or career — here, ironically, "an unhappy childhood" is being called the best "training" for a novelist.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "nature" does not fit; asking about the best "nature" for a novelist does not make sense, and "an unhappy childhood" is not an answer to a question about nature/temperament.

• Option 3: "medication" is unrelated to the context of becoming a novelist; "an unhappy childhood" is not medication.

• Option 4: "maintenance" does not fit the context of preparing to become a writer; it usually refers to the upkeep of machines or systems.

NOTE

• Cloze questions often require identifying the word that logically connects the blank to the sentence/quotation that follows it — here, the idea that suffering ("unhappy childhood") builds a writer's skill ("training").

• Related words: apprenticeship, grounding, schooling, groundwork.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. wondered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Redwing had enjoyed a fine time growing up, but he ________ if this whole expedition was unfolding more like a novel..." The blank requires a verb meaning to feel curious or to ask oneself something, followed by "if" (a typical construction for expressing doubt or curiosity).

• "Wondered" is correct because "wonder if" is a standard collocation meaning to feel curious or to question oneself about something.
◦ Example: She wondered if she had made the right decision.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "wasted" does not collocate with "if" in this sense and does not fit the meaning of questioning something.

• Option 3: "wandered" means to walk about aimlessly; it does not take the construction "wandered if" and is contextually about physical movement, not thought.

• Option 4: "welded" means to join metal pieces by heating; it is entirely unrelated to the context of thought or doubt.

NOTE

• The construction "wonder if/whether" is frequently tested in cloze passages to express doubt, curiosity, or a tentative question.

• Do not confuse "wonder" (to feel curious) with "wander" (to move about without a fixed direction) — a commonly tested pair in SSC vocabulary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...he wondered if this whole ________ was unfolding more like a novel..." Read alongside the passage's larger idea (that a person's life story — childhood through adulthood — can resemble the plot of a novel), the blank needs a noun referring to this life-journey as a whole undertaking.

• "Expedition" fits best among the given options as a noun describing an extended journey or undertaking, used here figuratively for the "journey" of Redwing's life, matching the passage's narrative, journey-like framing of a person's life.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "expiation" means the act of making amends for wrongdoing — it does not fit the context of a life story unfolding like a novel.

• Option 2: "expectation" means a belief that something will happen — it does not carry the sense of an ongoing, evolving undertaking that "unfolding" implies as clearly as "expedition" does.

• Option 3: "exasperation" means intense irritation — it does not fit the neutral, reflective tone of "wondered if this whole ___ was unfolding".

NOTE

• Cloze passages often test between similar-sounding words with the same "ex-" prefix but very different meanings: expiation (atonement), expectation (anticipation), exasperation (irritation), expedition (journey/undertaking) — always choose based on contextual meaning, not just similarity in spelling.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. based.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...and would be ________ on one person, one character, the guy in charge: him." The blank requires a word that collocates with the preposition "on" to mean grounded in or centred around something.

• "Based" is correct because "based on" is a standard collocation meaning "having as its foundation or main subject".
◦ Example: The novel would be based on one central character.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "bloomed" means to produce flowers or flourish; "bloomed on" is not a meaningful or standard collocation here.

• Option 3: "blessed" means endowed with divine favour; it does not collocate meaningfully with "on one person" in this sense.

• Option 4: "blamed" means held responsible for a fault; "blamed on" exists as a collocation, but it would give the illogical meaning that the novel is faulted onto one person, which does not fit the context of a novel's plot revolving around a central character.

NOTE

• "Based on" is a very common collocation tested in cloze passages, meaning founded upon or derived from.

• Similar-sounding "b-" words often confused in cloze tests: based, blessed, bloomed, blamed — always verify meaning through context, not just surface similarity.
